passages.t: The king comes on a colt
passages.happening: Jesus and his followers come near Jerusalem, to the villages of Bethphage and Bethany on the Mount of Olives. He sends two disciples ahead to find a young donkey, a colt that no one has ever ridden, tied up in the next village. If anyone asks, they are to say the Lord needs it and will send it back soon. It happens just as he said. They throw their cloaks on the colt and Jesus sits on it. Many people spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread branches cut from the fields. The crowd in front and behind shouts, “Hosanna!” and “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” Jesus enters Jerusalem and goes into the temple courts. He looks around at everything. It is late, so he goes back out to Bethany with the Twelve.
passages.hearers:
Bethany was a village a little under two miles from Jerusalem (John 11:18). Jesus stays there at night through the week. The Mount of Olives is the ridge just east of the city, looking across a valley at the temple.

The road would have been full. Jews came from many lands to Jerusalem for Passover, the feast that remembered how God set Israel free from slavery in Egypt. A feast about freedom, in a city ruled by Rome, could stir strong hopes.

Spreading cloaks on the road was a way to welcome a king. When Jehu was made king of Israel, the people put their garments under him and shouted, “Jehu is king!” (2 Kings 9:13). Branches were waved at times of victory too. When the Jewish leader Simon took back the fortress in Jerusalem in 141 BC, his people entered it with palm branches and songs (1 Maccabees 13:51).

‘Hosanna’ is a Hebrew word that first meant ‘Save us, please’. It comes from Psalm 118, one of the psalms of praise sung at the great feasts. By Jesus' day it had also become a shout of praise.

A king would ride a horse to war. Jesus chooses a young donkey.
passages.ot:
Mark does not quote it, but the prophet Zechariah had said, “See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). Matthew and John quote that verse at this point.

The crowd's words come from Psalm 118:26: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD.” The psalm's verse before it is the prayer “O LORD, save us, we pray.” And Zechariah had also said that on the day of the LORD, “His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4). Jesus comes into the city from that very hill.
passages.asks: The crowd wanted a king, and they were right that one had come. But he came gently, on a borrowed colt, and within a week many would turn away. Ask what kind of king you want Jesus to be, and whether you would still welcome him if he came humble instead of strong.

passages.t: A fig tree with only leaves
passages.happening: The next morning, leaving Bethany, Jesus is hungry. He sees a fig tree in leaf in the distance and goes to see if it has any fruit. He finds nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. He says to the tree, “May no one ever eat of your fruit again.” His disciples hear him say it.
passages.hearers:
Fig trees grew all over the land, and ‘sitting under your own fig tree’ was a picture of peace (Micah 4:4). Near Jerusalem the trees put out their leaves in spring, around Passover. Writers differ on whether small early figs come just before the leaves or with them, but a tree in full leaf could look as if it promised something to eat. The main crop of figs ripened in summer.

Mark tells his readers plainly that ‘it was not the season for figs’. He wants us to notice that this is not about a gardener losing his temper. It is a sign.

Mark also wraps this story around the next one. Fig tree, then temple, then fig tree again. When Mark sandwiches stories like this, each one helps explain the other.
passages.ot:
The prophets used the fig tree as a picture of God's people. Hosea remembered how God first saw Israel “as the firstfruits of the fig tree in its first season” (Hosea 9:10). Jeremiah, warning of judgment, said there would be “nor figs on the tree, and even the leaf will wither” (Jeremiah 8:13). Micah grieved that there was “no early fig that I crave” (Micah 7:1).

The prophets also acted out their messages. Jeremiah smashed a clay jar in front of the city's leaders to show what was coming (Jeremiah 19).
passages.hard:
Why would Jesus curse a tree for having no fruit when it was not even the season? The question is old and fair, and skeptics have long pressed it: the tree did nothing wrong.

Most Christian readers take Mark's own clues seriously. He says it was not the season, he places the tree around the scene in the temple, and the prophets had used the fig tree as a picture of God's people. So the cursing is read as an acted parable, a sign done in public, about a temple busy with worship but bearing no fruit for God. Some scholars think a parable Jesus told, like the one in Luke 13:6-9, was later told as an event. Others take it as an event that Jesus meant as a sign.

One caution matters a great deal. For centuries some Christians read the withered tree as God cursing the Jewish people. That reading fed contempt and cruelty. Jesus and his disciples were Jews, and so was the crowd that welcomed him. Mark aims the sign at the temple leadership in that hour, not at a people.
passages.asks: Leaves without fruit looks like life from far away. Ask where your faith might be all leaves: busy, visible, and religious, but bearing little of the love, honesty, and mercy God looks for. The question is for every reader, not for someone else.

passages.happening: In Jerusalem Jesus goes into the temple courts and begins to drive out those who are buying and selling there. He overturns the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. He will not let anyone carry goods through the temple courts. Then he teaches them: “Is it not written: ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’” The chief priests and scribes hear it and look for a way to kill him. They are afraid of him, because the whole crowd is amazed at his teaching. That evening Jesus and his disciples leave the city.
passages.hearers:
The temple was the centre of Jewish life, the one place where sacrifices were offered to God. In Jesus' day it was a vast building, and work on it had gone on for decades (John 2:20). Its huge outer court was open to everyone, including non-Jews, called Gentiles. A low stone barrier marked how far a Gentile could go. In 1871 a stone was found with a Greek warning on it: a foreigner who went past the barrier would have only himself to blame for his death.

The trade Jesus disrupted met real needs. Every Jewish man paid a half shekel each year for the temple (Exodus 30:13), and the temple took it in one kind of coin, the silver shekel of Tyre. So pilgrims had to change their money. The Mishnah, written down around AD 200, says the money changers set up tables in the temple three weeks or so before Passover (Shekalim 1:3).

Doves were the offering of the poor. A person who could not afford a lamb brought two doves or pigeons instead (Leviticus 5:7; 12:8). The Mishnah remembers a time when a pair of doves cost a gold coin in Jerusalem, until a leading teacher, Rabban Simeon ben Gamaliel, changed a ruling and the price fell (Keritot 1:7). So prices for the poor could be a real worry.

The Mishnah also says no one should use the temple mount as a shortcut (Berakhot 9:5). That may help explain why Jesus stops people carrying goods through the courts.
passages.ot:
Jesus joins two prophets. Isaiah 56:7 promises that foreigners who love God will come to his temple, “for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations.” Jeremiah stood in the temple gate and warned people who felt safe because the temple was there. God asked, “Has this house, which bears My Name, become a den of robbers in your sight?” (Jeremiah 7:11). A den is where robbers hide after their crimes. Jeremiah's point was that people sinned all week and then ran to the temple as if it would keep them safe.

Malachi had promised that “the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to His temple” (Malachi 3:1).
passages.hard:
What was Jesus doing? Christians and scholars read the scene in a few ways. Some see a cleansing: Jesus protests against greed and unfair trade in God's house and calls it back to prayer. Some see a sign of judgment: like Jeremiah, Jesus acts out the end of the temple, and the fig tree around the scene points the same way. Some stress the words ‘for all the nations’: the place where Gentiles could pray had been filled with trade. These readings can overlap, and many hold more than one.

John tells of Jesus clearing the temple near the start of his work (John 2:13-22), while Mark puts it in the last week. Some think it happened twice. Others think John placed one event early for reasons of his own. These notes do not settle it.

This was not Jesus attacking his own people's faith. He was a Jew speaking inside Israel's own tradition, as Jeremiah had, about the house of his Father. And Mark notes that the crowd, the ordinary Jewish worshippers, hung on his words.
passages.asks: Jesus was zealous that the poor, the outsider, and the person who simply wanted to pray could reach God. Ask whether anything in your church, or in you, makes it harder for others to come near. Ask too whether you treat worship as a safe place to hide from changing how you live.

passages.happening: The next morning they pass the fig tree again. It has withered from the roots. Peter remembers and says, “Look, Rabbi! The fig tree You cursed has withered.” Jesus answers, “Have faith in God.” Truly, if anyone says to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart but believes it will happen, it will be done. So whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. And when you stand to pray, if you hold anything against anyone, forgive them, so that your Father in heaven will forgive you too.
passages.hearers:
The road from Bethany runs over the Mount of Olives, with the temple mount in view across the valley. So when Jesus says ‘this mountain’, many readers think he means the mountain the temple stood on. Others read ‘moving mountains’ simply as a common picture for doing what seems impossible.

Jews often prayed standing up, as Jesus says here (verse 25). Hannah stood to pray (1 Samuel 1:26), and so did the tax collector in Jesus' story (Luke 18:13).

You may notice that your Bible skips from verse 25 to verse 27. Verse 26, ‘But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in heaven forgive your trespasses’, is missing from the oldest manuscripts, including Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. It closely matches Matthew 6:15 and was probably copied in from there. Older English Bibles such as the King James Version print it. Nothing is lost, because Jesus says the same thing in Matthew.
passages.hard:
Does Jesus promise that we will get anything we ask for if we believe hard enough? Some teachers have said so, and have told people that unanswered prayer means weak faith. That has hurt many who prayed for a sick child or a broken marriage and did not see it healed.

Most Christian traditions read the words in their setting. They begin with ‘Have faith in God’, not faith in your own certainty. They end at once with forgiving others, which ties prayer to the heart of the one praying. Elsewhere Jesus teaches us to pray ‘your will be done’ (Matthew 6:10), and in the garden of Gethsemane he himself asks for the cup to pass and then accepts that it will not (14:36). Paul asked three times for his ‘thorn’ to be taken away and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). So the promise is read as a call to bold prayer to a Father who can do anything, not a tool for making God do what we want. Skeptics fairly ask what it means if the plain words fail. The Gospel itself does not hide that its central figure prayed and was crucified.
passages.asks: Is there something you have stopped asking God for because it seems impossible? Jesus invites bold prayer. Then he points straight at your grudges. Ask who you need to forgive before you pray again.

passages.happening: Back in Jerusalem, Jesus is walking in the temple courts. The chief priests, scribes, and elders come to him and ask, “By what authority are You doing these things?” Who gave him that right? Jesus says he will answer if they answer one question first. John's baptism: was it from heaven or from men? They talk it over. If they say ‘from heaven’, he will ask why they did not believe John. If they say ‘from men’, they fear the crowd, because everyone held that John was truly a prophet. So they answer, “We do not know.” Jesus replies that neither will he tell them by what authority he does these things.
passages.hearers:
The chief priests, scribes, and elders were the leaders who made up the council in Jerusalem. The temple was their charge. A Galilean teacher had just disrupted its business, so their question is a fair one from where they stood.

Jesus answers with a question of his own, as he did with the Pharisees about divorce (10:3). It is not a dodge. Jesus' question is the answer, if they will see it. John had pointed to Jesus. If John's work came from God, so does the authority of the one John announced.

‘From heaven’ was a respectful Jewish way of saying ‘from God’.
passages.ot: John came as the messenger promised by Malachi, who would prepare the way (Malachi 3:1), and Mark opened his book with those words (1:2). Now the Lord has come to his temple, and its leaders do not know what to say.
passages.asks: The leaders could not answer because they were weighing what was safe, not what was true. Ask whether you ever do the same: deciding what you believe about Jesus by what it would cost you, or what others would think.
